description: How Chrome ate the web: a 2006–2025 market-share chart race that shows one browser's meteoric ascent and Internet Explorer's collapse.
youtube_description:
00:00 Intro — The Browser Race in 60 seconds
00:25 2006–2009 — IE rules, Firefox rises, Chrome appears
01:05 2010–2012 — Chrome surges, IE cracks
02:00 2013–2016 — Chrome becomes dominant, Edge arrives
02:45 2017–2020 — Mobile and Safari growth; IE collapses
03:30 2021–2025 — The modern web: Chrome at ~64%, IE near 1%
04:00 Closing thoughts & sources

Story: This visualization tracks global browser market share from 2006 to 2025. In 2006 Internet Explorer controlled roughly 74% of the market while Chrome didn’t exist; by 2012 Chrome passed IE (Chrome ~32% vs IE ~34%) and then exploded — reaching ~59% by 2015 and stabilizing around ~64% through 2025. Internet Explorer fell from ~74% in 2006 to ~1% in 2025, effectively crushed by the rise of Chrome, mobile browsing (Safari), and Microsoft’s pivot to Edge.

Why it matters: Chrome’s rapid adoption (0%→~64% in under two decades) rewired web development, privacy debates, and ad ecosystems. Legacy IE’s collapse forced enterprise migrations, massive compatibility rewrites, and the end of ActiveX-era web design.

Sources: StatCounter Global Stats (browser market share by year), NetMarketShare historical archives, W3Counter and official company blogs (Google, Microsoft, Mozilla). Exact year-by-year values compiled from public global market-share snapshots.

instagram_caption:
🚀 The browser that ate the internet: Chrome went from 0% in 2008 to ~64% by 2025 while Internet Explorer fell from 74% in 2006 to just ~1%.

The story in three acts: In 2006 the web was dominated by Internet Explorer (~74%) with Firefox and Safari nibbling around the edges. Chrome’s launch in 2008 was quiet at first — 2.5% that year — but by 2012 Chrome had surged to ~32% and narrowly overtook IE, which had slipped to ~34%. That moment triggered a two-decade tectonic shift.

Act II is acceleration. From 2012 to 2016 Chrome rocketed from ~32% to ~63%. Developers rewrote apps for a Chromium engine, extensions boomed, and Google’s browser became the default on millions of new Android devices. Microsoft tried to respond: IE’s share plunged (19% in 2014 → 13% in 2015) and Edge debuted in 2015 to replace IE in Windows 10 — but it never reclaimed the top spot.

Act III is consolidation. By 2020 Chrome sat near ~64%, Safari grew with mobile to ~16%, Firefox softened to ~7%, and Edge carved out a steady ~10% by 2025. The headline: a single browser came to dominate both desktop and mobile web experiences, reshaping privacy, extensions, and how sites are built.

Headline: How Chrome Won the Browser Wars — A 2006–2025 Timeline

Summary: This visualization shows the dramatic shift in global browser market share. In 2006 Internet Explorer held roughly 74% of the market. Chrome launched in 2008 and climbed rapidly to ~32% by 2012, overtaking IE as it declined. By 2015 Chrome reached ~59% and stabilized around ~64% through 2025. Internet Explorer’s share collapsed to about 1% by 2025. Safari and Edge grew steadily (Safari with mobile, Edge as Microsoft’s replacement), while Firefox declined from its early peak.

Context: The data reflects major industry events: Chrome’s introduction (2008), the mobile browser surge led by Safari (iPhone adoption), Microsoft’s shift from IE to Edge (2015), and the long-term consolidation around Chromium engines.

Sources: StatCounter Global Stats, NetMarketShare, company reports from Google, Microsoft, and Mozilla.
